newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean prosecutors, employers in union crackdown.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean prosecutors, employers in union crackdown.

text.p: Labour strikes erupted in South Korea with new ferocity on Monday as state prosecutors and management of giant industrial conglomerates launched an offensive against union leaders.
Almost 150,000 workers walked out, idling carmakers and shipbuilding yards, as the government and employers squared off for a bruising battle with organised labour.
Hospital workers that had earlier given up strike action against a new labour law said they would return to the fray on Tuesday. Broadcast unions and white-collar workers are scheduled to join them.
Prosecutors summoned leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions to appear for questioning over the strikes, which have been declared illegal.
The confederation said it would defy the order as its leaders huddled in a makeshift tent pitched on the snow-covered grounds of Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.
The country's five main employers' groups announced they would sue union chiefs for losses they estimated at 340 billion won ($403 million) since strikes began on December 26.

Senior prosecutor Lee Sang-hyong said about 20 leaders of the Korean Confederation were ordered to appear by Tuesday. But confederation president Kwon Young-kil told a news conference: "We will not respond."
Kwon threatened to escalate industrial action unless President Kim Young-sam announced a repeal of the new law at a news conference scheduled for Tuesday.
He said workers at hospitals, broadcasters and medical insurance firms would join in unless Kim backed down.

Later, the Korean Federation of Hospitals Workers Union said members at 24 medical centres, including Seoul National University Hospital, would walk out at dawn on Tuesday even before Kim's news conference.

The confederation claims membership of around 500,000 workers. Its larger counterpart, the Korean Federation of Trade Unions, claims 1.2 million members and its leaders were meeting to discuss their next move after earlier calling off strikes until January 11.

The new law, rammed through parliament with no debate on December 26, allows employers to sack workers, eroding decades of near-total job security. It also enables companies to replace strikers and hire temporary staff.
Kwon accused the government of trying to divert public attention from the industrial unrest by provoking a showdown between unions and public prosecutors.
"Despite the government's strong response we will push on with our strikes and we won't back down," Kwon said.
Employers, who have tried conciliation to assuage union angers, said they would hold union leaders personally responsible for strike damage.

"We will sue those who have led illegal actions at production sites," Byun Hae-ryong, a director of the Korea Employers' Federation, told reporters after a meeting of representatives from five leading employers' groups and the country's top 15 conglomerates.
About 10,000 workers poured into a downtown Seoul park to vent their fury against moves on their unions, witnesses said.

Hyundai Motor Co Ltd and 12 other Hyundai Group affiliates, including Hyundai Mipo Dockyard Co Ltd, began an indefinite strike affecting 73,341 union workers, a union official said. Hyundai Group has 20 unions.
Daewoo Motor Co Ltd, Daewoo Heavy Industries -- which operates a shipyard -- and four other Daewoo Group units were also idled after 27,650 unionised workers walked out.
Production lines at Kia Motors were at a standstill as 18,000 workers continued strike action. Ssangyong Motor Co's 7,853 union workers voted to resume their walkout.

White-collar workers at government-backed research institutes and industry associations joined in under the banner of the Korea Federation of Professional and Technicians Unions that represents 14,256 staff.
Stocks tumbled on fears that action against unions could further inflame some of the worst industrial unrest since the late 1980s. The leading index closed down 2.5 percent.
